lines: Watch the timing here, not the outcome. Two operators, the same file, eight seconds apart. Neither one sees an error on their screen.
The second plan was already wrong the moment it was computed — it just didn't know that yet.
Before I answer, think about what a plan would even need to compare against to make this kind of mistake possible.
Of these four options, which one is actually sitting between your configuration and your real infrastructure?
answer: Its own last-known record — not the live cloud, checked fresh.
Which means the plan is only ever as current as that record. Let the record go stale, and the plan goes stale with it.

lines: Notice what this box is not. It isn't a live connection to your cloud account, refreshed on demand.
It's a written-down memory of the last thing the tool actually did — and every future plan trusts that memory completely.
Watch the second request fail, not stall. There's no queue here, no retry, no race that sometimes goes the other way.
One holder, one lock. The second operator simply cannot start until the first one is done.
Resist the urge to treat plan as a formality on the way to apply. Nothing in the real world changes while this box is open.
Apply is the only step that touches anything — which is exactly why reviewing the plan, not the apply, is where a mistake actually gets caught.
Here's the part worth sitting with: these two aren't opposite problems, they're the same gap, just discovered from different sides.
One notices reality already moved. The other deliberately catches the tool up to it, without tearing anything down to do it.
Don't mistake this for a technical requirement. Nothing forces these three into one unit — grouping them is a decision about what one review has to cover.
Split them into three, and someone can change the role without anyone reviewing the bucket it protects.
Notice what actually changed here. Not the tool's behavior that day — the legal terms underneath using it.
That distinction is the whole reason a fork was even a reasonable response, instead of just reading the fine print more carefully.
Watch what this buys you: real loops, real conditionals, the full power of an actual language describing your infrastructure.
Now watch what it costs. That same power can write imperative logic that quietly breaks the very safety story a plan is supposed to guarantee.
Notice this isn't a suggestion with a comment thread attached. The plan simply does not reach apply.
A rule that can be ignored is a guideline. A rule that blocks the plan itself is something else entirely.
If you only remember one line: the record can go stale, which is why a lock matters, and a policy gate is the only one of these that reads the plan's own content.
State, lock, plan, apply, drift, import, policy gate — seven ideas, one underlying story about trusting a record instead of reality.
Before I answer, notice this plan already shipped — the question isn't how to detect it after the fact, it's what would have stopped it before.
Of everything covered, which mechanism actually reads a plan's content and can refuse it?
answer: A policy-as-code gate — the only mechanism here that inspects what the plan actually contains.
Locking only stops two operators from colliding. It was never going to stop one operator's single, perfectly uncontested, bad plan.
